dialog.body: Public Works, this is Lorraine, how can I help you this morning?

Yes, good morning. My name is Carlos Resendes. I'm calling about the storm drain on my corner. It backed up in that storm, Friday into Saturday, and the water came right into my basement. And I'll tell you, I've been waiting all weekend to get somebody on the phone.
I'm sorry, Mr. Resendes. Let me get this down. What's the address?
Fourteen Wellington Avenue. That's... one, four. Wellington Avenue. In the Fifth Ward. The drain is right there at the corner, near my house.
Fourteen Wellington Avenue. And the drain's at the corner by you. Okay. And this was during the coastal storm, Friday and Saturday?

Overnight Friday into Saturday. Saturday the tenth. My husband went down in the morning and he called me, he says, Carlos, come look. And there was water all over the floor. About six inches. Six inches of water, in a finished basement.
About six inches. Do you know where it came in?

Two places. It came up through the floor drain, and it came in the window well. The glass, on the street side. The window well filled up and it came through the glass. Because the street had nowhere to go. That drain at the corner, it was full. Backed up. Nothing was going down it.
Okay, so the floor drain and the window well on the street side. And you could see the corner drain was backed up.

You could see it from my front window. The water on the street was up to your ankles. Ankle deep. And the cars, they keep driving through like it's nothing, and they're throwing a wake, like a boat. Right up onto the sidewalk, right toward my house. Nobody slows down. And that drain, I look at it, there's leaves, there's sand, there's all kinds of stuff in it. It's been like that. Somebody should have been cleaning it before a storm like this. They knew the storm was coming. Everybody knew.
I hear you. I'm writing down that there's debris in the grate and the street was ponding ankle deep. What got damaged down there, if you know yet?

We have a spare refrigerator down there. That was sitting in the water. I don't know if it's going to work, I unplugged it, I'm afraid to plug it back in. And the holiday decorations. We just put them all away, after New Year's. The boxes were on the floor and they're soaked. Cardboard, everything. My husband spent Saturday carrying it all out to the garage to dry.
So the spare refrigerator and the holiday decorations got wet. Okay.

And I want to say, I'm not blaming you, miss. But this is the city's drain. It's not my drain. I take care of my house, I clean my gutters, I do what I'm supposed to do. And then the city's drain is plugged and the water comes in my house. That's not right. Somebody has to come and look at it. Not next month. Now. Before the next one.

That's fair. I'm going to put in a work order for a drain backup at the corner by fourteen Wellington, and I'll have a crew go check the grate and the catch basin. Give me one second here. [pause] Okay. The earliest I can get a crew out there is Wednesday, the fourteenth.
Wednesday. So two more days. And Saturday was the storm. So it sits there almost a week before anybody even looks at it.

I know it's not what you want to hear. After a storm like that we've got calls coming in from all over, and the crews are going street to street. But you're on the list for Wednesday, the fourteenth, and they'll check the corner.
You probably hear this all day, huh? People calling, my basement, my street, my this. You must have the phone ringing off the wall since Saturday.
It's been a busy morning, I won't lie to you. But that's what we're here for.

Well. I'm sorry you have to listen to all of us. But I want this written down, so I'm not calling back in two weeks and nobody knows what I'm talking about. Can you give me a number? A work order number, or a reference, something?
Absolutely. Do you have a pen?
Hold on. [pause] Okay. Go ahead. Slow, please.
Sure. It's W-O, then two, six, zero, one, one, two, dash, zero, four, seven.
W-O. Two... six... zero... one... one... two. Dash. Zero... four... seven. Is that right?
That's right. W-O two six zero one one two, dash zero four seven.
Okay. I have it. I'm going to put it on the refrigerator. The good one, upstairs.
Good idea. And can I get a phone number for the work order, in case we need to reach you?
Yes. It's the house phone. Four... zero... one. Five... five... five. Zero... one... one... one.
Four oh one, five five five, oh one one one. And the name again, Resendes, is that R-E-S-E-N-D-E-S?
That's it. Carlos.

Okay, Mr. Resendes. So I've got it down: drain backup at the corner by fourteen Wellington Avenue, water came in through the floor drain and the street-side window well, about six inches overnight Friday into Saturday the tenth, spare refrigerator and holiday decorations got wet, street was ankle deep. Crew to check the corner Wednesday the fourteenth.
Yes. And put in there about the cars. The wakes. Because even if the drain is a little bit slow, when the cars go by, it pushes the water right at the houses. That's half the problem.
I'll add that. Cars throwing wakes toward the houses when it ponds.
Thank you. And Wednesday, they're going to clean it, or they're going to look at it?
They'll go out and check the grate and the basin, and clear what they can. If they find something bigger going on underneath, they'll write it up from there.

Okay. Because I don't want somebody to come, look, scratch the head, and go away. I want it fixed. Fourteen years in this house, I never had water on that basement floor like that. Never. So something's wrong with that drain.
Understood. I'll make a note that you want it cleared, not just looked at.
Alright. Wednesday. I'll be watching out the window.
If Wednesday comes and goes and nobody shows, you call us back with that work order number and we'll find out what happened.
Oh, I'll call. Don't worry about that. Thank you, Lorraine.
You're welcome, Mr. Resendes. I hope the refrigerator comes back. Take care.
We'll see. Goodbye.
